paper.title: Keying Hash Functions for Message Authentication (HMAC); test vectors from RFC 4231
paper.venue: CRYPTO 1996 (specified as RFC 2104; test vectors in RFC 4231 by M. Nystrom)

program.how: written for ounce-core from the HMAC definition (RFC 2104) and the SHA-224/256/384/512 descriptions of FIPS 180-4; the SHA-2 round constants and initial values are computed in the program from their mathematical definition (fractional bits of cube and square roots of primes, integer big-number arithmetic) rather than typed in. No third-party code copied
program.target: static freestanding aarch64 Linux ELF, run with `ounce-core run-elf`

claims_checked: RFC 4231 test cases 1 to 7 (keys of 4, 20, 25 and 131 bytes, data of 8 to 152 bytes, including keys longer than the block size and one truncated-to-128-bit case) for HMAC-SHA-224, HMAC-SHA-256, HMAC-SHA-384 and HMAC-SHA-512: 28 of 28 values match
as a by-product the derived SHA-2 constants are right, since any wrong constant would change every HMAC value

expected_values_source.what: the HMAC-SHA-2 test vectors of RFC 4231 section 4, parsed mechanically from the fetched RFC text (key and data lengths cross-checked against the RFC's own '(N bytes)' annotations)
expected_values_source.note: the vectors are data, copied as numbers. The 1996 paper itself and the HMAC-MD5 / HMAC-SHA-1 vectors of RFC 2202 were not used

negative_control: built with -DHMAC_IPAD=0x37 (inner pad byte 0x37 instead of 0x36), 0 of 28 values match and the program exits 1; check.sh reports NOT REPRODUCED
not_checked: the paper's security proof (HMAC as a PRF / MAC given the compression function's properties)
HMAC-MD5 and HMAC-SHA-1, SHA-3 based HMAC, and SHA-2 hashes on their own (only HMAC outputs are compared; the NIST SHA known-answer files were not fetched)
truncation other than test case 5's 128 bits, and messages longer than 152 bytes
speed figures (emulator run time says nothing about any hardware)
Tier-4 and native ARM64 execution (the native comparison is x86-64)
what_a_pass_means: this program, run on ounce-core, produces exactly RFC 4231's HMAC-SHA-2 values for its seven test cases. It does not show HMAC is secure.
